A 2018 study published in the ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing demonstrated that using open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing makes field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies.
Many earlier global land cover products relied on imagery at 250 meters to 1 kilometer resolution, but Landsat-8 imagery offers 30-meter pixels fine enough to resolve individual fields in many agricultural areas. The 2018 study produced high-accuracy, 30-meter extent maps for cropland in Australia and China.
The output was a binary map distinguishing cropland from everything else, produced separately for each country and assessed against independent reference data. Among the surprising findings was that cropland mapping of Australia and China can be accomplished using the same algorithm.
Landsat-8 revisits each location about every 16 days, allowing the study to capture how croplands are managed throughout the growing season. The study used Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE). Read more about the hows and whys in the paper.
Australia (top left) and China (top right) have dramatically different agricultural landscapes, but the same algorithm can map cropland in both. Field-scale mapping of cropland can now be accomplished using the same algorithm for countries with vastly different agricultural landscapes. [Teluguntla et al., 2018]
So what are the implications? Well, water allocation is a constant concern in Australia, and groundwater depletion is a serious issue in northern China. This paper gives decision makers valuable insight into how to monitor cropland in their respective countries.
The findings also demonstrate that the open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing make field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies.
The paper:
Teluguntla, Sensing, et al. 2018. Fine-scale mapping of croplands using Landsat-8 data, Google Earth Engine and machine learning. ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing 2018.

These centers would provide poor and orphaned children with an opportunity to play, learn, eat, and access basic health care, and offer mothers and guardians knowledge and skills to build more stable lives. The plan is to provide support services like basic health care, vocational and small-business skills training leading to more stable income and greater independence, as well as safe-motherhood education on prenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal recovery, family planning, and newborn care, especially for young and first-time mothers.
The initiative includes partnerships with local government and community structures to align these centers with public services and child-protection systems, as well as schools and educators to support learning and ease the transition into formal education.
The innovative approach helps poor and orphaned children—the lifeblood of communities like these—engage in their futures in ways that their parents have not been able to do.
Support services for poor and orphaned children
Imagine a child living in one of these neighborhoods, a child who has no health facilities or practitioners in his neighborhood, who must walk for miles to see a physician or get his immunization shots. One child we know had to walk 1080 meters (1080 yards) to the nearest health facility and an equally long distance to get to school. Parents are reluctant to send their children to school when they need to live in fear of disease and injury. Instead, they send them to play outside, in narrow lanes that double as playgrounds but are also open drainage channels that run past their doorways.
In the neighborhoods we visit, children don’t have a place to play or learn, a place where they can eat or get basic health care, a place where their mothers and guardians can learn how to build more stable lives. Instead, they play on the streets, where their chances of injury, disease, or worse are high. This child’s parents might just be struggling to get enough money to feed him, let alone to send him to school. The child might be orphaned, abandoned, or living in a survival situation, with no one to take care of him. Until now, these children have nowhere to go, no place to play, learn, eat, or get basic health care.
A child who lives in a situation like this can’t imagine his future. His parents don’t have the opportunity to build a better life for him. The initiative we’re proposing changes that by offering a support system of basic health care, vocational and small-business skills training, and safe-motherhood education, all in one center. The plan is a network of community resource centers built inside or next to the neighborhoods they serve.
The centers would offer basic health care: growth monitoring, immunization follow-up, deworming, first aid, and referrals to clinics and hospitals. Border collies were developed to herd sheep, but they are also good family pets. However, the same qualities that make border collies good family pets can also present some challenges, so it’s important for owners to understand the breed before getting a border collie.

Border Collie Breed
Border collies are not like other dog breeds. Because they have been bred for a specific purpose for centuries, they have unique qualities that are not only different than other dog breeds but also different than dogs in general.
Border collies are herding dogs, which means they were bred to herd livestock, particularly sheep.
The origins of the border collie breed lie in the borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17/19 centuries. Although the border collie has been recognized as a distinct breed for only the last century or so, there are many dogs that are descendants of the first border collies.
For many years, border collies were bred by shepherds who needed dogs that could help them herd sheep. Border collies were matched with the working qualities that the shepherd wanted to strengthen. While many shepherds were very careful to only breed to achieve the qualities they wanted, Adam Telfer, a shepherd working in the 19 century, is often credited with helping to consolidate the border collie type by deliberately crossbreeding his dogs.

Telfer’s descendants became the foundation of the modern breed. Later, celebrated herding dogs can be traced back to this lineage.

A Student’s Education
Students learn from more than the curriculum taught. They learn from how a teacher treats a struggling classmate, how the teacher handles a conflict, or how the teacher responds to a hard question. From the way a teacher speaks to a student who comes to school hungry, to how the teacher reacts to the news that someone has been bullied, to the way a teacher sees opportunity when it seems that there’s only a problem—students learn from what teachers do, and how they do it.
Because of that, the Diocese of Richmond’s Consensus Curriculum is a framework for our Catholic schools—not a strict script we follow. We begin with the faith—the lens through which every subject in the Consensus Curriculum is taught—and then allow the curriculum to lead us to teachable moments that allow our students to learn.
Our students learn from their teachers’ example of faithfulness and from the way that teachers live out the Catholic faith in the classrooms, on the playgrounds, and in the hallways of our schools.
Our curriculum is organized by grade level so that younger-year content includes self-worth, friendship, and family relationships, but as students grow older, we introduce more complex topics that can then be explored more deeply as they get older. Here’s a snapshot of the topics covered in the Consensus Curriculum:
Our “Catholic Curriculum”
Social Studies: Our Social Studies curriculum covers everything from history, geography, civics, and economics, including Virginia and U.S. history. We teach about human dignity, justice, and the common good through our history units—and we use history to open questions about conscience, sacrifice, and redemption through novels.
Language Arts: Language Arts has a lot of opportunity for our teachers to reach our students. Younger-year students can be taught about the importance of friendship through literature, and as they get older, our Language Arts curriculum helps them learn about themselves and what it means to be human through works of fiction and non-fiction.
Science: We use our Science curriculum to help our students learn about the natural world—and to help them wonder at the order of creation. We also use our Science curriculum to help our students learn about the dignity of human life, and how we are called to be stewards of creation.
Religion: Our Religion curriculum is foundational to the work we do in all of our classrooms. We focus on building our students’ relationship with God, and the relationship our students have with each other and with our community. We also use our Religion curriculum to help our students understand what it means to be human, and how they are called to live their lives.
Mathematics: Our Mathematics curriculum is the building blocks that helps our students build their own understanding of the world. We can use Mathematics to help our students learn about justice, fairness, and human dignity, and we can also help them learn about God’s order by helping them understand the importance of sequence and pattern.
Music: Music can help our students understand God’s love, and it can also help them explore the order and beauty of creation. It can help them learn to express themselves, and can teach them that everyone has a purpose.
Physical Education: Our Physical Education curriculum helps our students learn that all human beings are created with dignity, and that everyone has a purpose. It can also teach our students about teamwork and how to work together in pursuit of a common goal.
Art: Our Article curriculum helps our students learn to explore their own creativity, and as they get older, can help them learn to use their creativity to express themselves. It can help them learn that God has created each of them with a special purpose, and that everyone has a role to play.
Technology: Our Technology curriculum gives our students the opportunity to learn about how they can live their lives as responsible, digital citizens. It can help them explore the beauty of creation, and the ways that God has created them to use their gifts. It can also help them learn the importance of community, and how their role is an important part of the whole.
Foreign Language: Our foreign Language curriculum helps our students learn about the importance of communication, and how they can use language to express themselves. They can learn to communicate in different ways, and to understand that God created them with a special role to play in the world.
Part of our Diocese’s Catholic Curriculum is the Benziger Family Life Series, a program that helps address human growth, relationships, and family life from a Catholic perspective. As our students get older, we can help them learn how to navigate the complexities of human life, and how their understanding of the world can help them make sense of the complexity.
Our Catholic curriculum allows us to teach our students from a place of faith—our teachers, our curriculum, our resources, and our programs are all designed to help our students learn to love and serve God and neighbor.
Our curriculum is the foundation for what our students learn, but it’s not the only way that our students learn. They learn from the way that we teach, from the way that we live out our faith, and from the way that we help them navigate the complexities of the world.
It’s why we’re committed to serving our students with excellence, and committed to helping our students learn what it means to live a life of faith and discipleship.
If you’d like to learn more about our Catholic curriculum, or want to know how we can help your student learn, please contact our school office and we’d be happy to answer any questions you have.

A small Perthshire town on the banks of the River Tay, Dunkeld is known as an important ecclesiastical centre in early medieval Scotland. With its centre made up of whitewashed cottages with neat gables and a cathedral by the water, Dunkeld is a picturesque place, although one with a turbulent history. In the wake of the Battle of Killiecrankie in 1689, Jacobite Highlanders and the Cameronian regiment fought here, and much of the town was burned down. Dunkeld’s cathedral, in its present form, dates largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries, but following the battle the cathedral choir remained in use as the parish church, while the ruined nave stood beside it.
The Atholl Memorial Fountain
In the centre of the square of Dunkeld, a stone fountain stands. It commemorates George Murray, 6 th Duke of Atholl who died in 1864. The fountain is a memorial to the man’s great act of public service to Dunkeld – bringing piped water to the town. Before the 6 th Duke brought piped water, the water running to the homes of Dunkeld was a gift of the Atholl estate. The title Duke of Atholl was created in 1703, and the Atholl seat was Blair Castle, to the north of Dunkeld. The 4 th Duke of Atholl was a powerful presence in the district when Telford’s bridge across the Tay was completed in 1809. He was known as the “Planter Duke”, for his planting of vast numbers of larches and other conifers across the Atholl lands.
Dunkeld’s Little Houses
Just off the Highlanders’ road, a short way along the main road out of Dunkeld, there is a row of small, sturdy cottages known as the “Little Houses”. These cottages were restored in the twentieth century by the National Trust for Scotland. Like much of the rest of Dunkeld, the “Little Houses” were badly damaged during the battle at Killiecrankie. The 6 th Duke’s great act of public service to Dunkeld wasn’t just bringing piped water to the town. The 4 th Duke had also planted vast numbers of larches and other conifers across the Atholl lands. These were planted to prevent erosion of the land, but they also add a wilder, more mysterious touch to the Atholl lands, and the act of planting them was a powerful one.
A suggested visit
You could start your visit to Dunkeld at the fountain in the centre of the town. The people of Dunkeld chose a fountain, a structure that delivers water, as the memorial to the Duke, rather than a statue. After seeing the fountain, following the streets down to the cathedral and Telford’s bridge should take less than an hour. A non-profit organization supplied office products to its member agencies: paper, pens, toner, folders, and similar staples. Suppliers shipped products to the center, the center stored them, and staff picked orders and shipped them to the agencies.
The center was not necessary on its own because the order-tracking function could run through suppliers or software. In fact, the center’s information function had no intrinsic value. It was only valuable in the context of the physical operations that drove the need to track the orders: receiving, putting away, picking, and shipping. Without the physical operation, the information would not be necessary.
In that context, the center added a step: every item was received, put away, picked, packed, and shipped a second time. That meant extra labor, extra space, extra inventory on the balance sheet, and extra days in lead time.
The center failed storage because demand was not only steady, it was predictable. Inventory turned over quickly, so there was no real buffer to hold against a surge or shortage.
The center failed consolidation because combining goods did not give any meaningful freight savings. Suppliers already packed the office goods in the quantities that the agencies bought, so nothing needed to be broken down into smaller lots.
The center did not fail assembly because it did not put together mixed shipments from many distant sources in a way that cut freight costs.
The center did not fail information because agencies received the same products they could have received directly from the supplier, but later and at higher cost.
The center failed break-bulk because goods arrived in customer-ready quantities. Nothing needed to be broken down into smaller lots.
The center failed customization because there was no on-site value-added work. No kitting, labeling, or special packaging happened at the center.
The sensible answer in this case was elimination: have suppliers ship directly to the agencies, or use a distributor that already offers consolidated delivery. Then the non-profit organization could focus on negotiating prices and coordinating service.
When Is a Distribution Center a Goods idea?
In the above example, the distribution center failed to add value. In fact, it added cost. So the logical decision was to eliminate it.
Some businesses are tempted to jump on the bandwagon and set up their own distribution center. They dream of consolidation, cutting transportation costs, squeezing out the “middleman,” and other benefits.
However, distribution centers can add cost as well as value. And, if they add cost, they should be eliminated.
So, when is a distribution center a good idea?
The best approach to answering that question is to try to decide if a distribution center adds value.
If you can’t come up with a good answer to that question, the sensible thing to do is to get rid of the distribution center.
One good approach is to break down the potential benefits into the five basic functions of distribution centers (see figure). In each case, ask if your distribution center adds value in that function.
If you can’t come up with a good answer, your distribution center is costing you money that you could save by getting rid of it.
The five basic functions are:
Consolidation
Storage
Break-bulk
Information
Customization
Consolidation
This is the process of combining goods from many sources into shipments that can take advantage of the transportation network. If your goods arrive in different lots that you combine into a shipment that takes advantage of the transportation network, your distribution center could add value. Think about the difference between buying one widget from a supplier and buying a truckload of widgets from that supplier. The widget might cost $1040, while the truckload might cost $1, 3 though you can only buy one widget at a time.
If you have different suppliers and could combine their goods into a freight-consolidated shipment, that’s another way in which your distribution center might add value. Think of it this way: you could get your widget from the supplier or you could get your widget from a distributor that already combines goods from many suppliers into consolidated shipments that take advantage of the transportation network.
Information
If you’re running your own distribution center to serve your agencies, you have your own information function. Ask yourself if that information is necessary on its own, or if it only has value in the context of the physical operations that drive the need to track the orders.
Think about what you’d lose if your information function had to go away. If you couldn’t track the orders, what would that mean for your ability to receive the goods, put them away, pick them, pack them, and ship them? Would you lose the ability to do those things? Then you’d lose your distribution center.
Or would you be able to do those things, but in a more expensive way? Would you be able to track the orders by running them through suppliers or software? If so, your distribution center might add value in its information function.
If your distribution center’s information function is only necessary in the context of the physical operations, that’s a good indicator that your distribution center might add value in that function. If it’s only necessary on its own, that’s a good indicator that your distribution center might not add value in that function.
Break-bulk
This is the process of breaking your shipments down into smaller lots that customers will buy. Think about buying office supplies. They’re not seasonal, perishable, or speculative, so there’s no real buffer to hold against a surge or shortage. Suppliers already pack office goods in the quantities that the agencies buy, so nothing needs to be broken down into smaller lots.

The answer is that it depends on your age, your underlying blood pressure status, whether your doctor has ordered it, what other risks you have, and what your medical needs are.
Sometimes blood pressure can get pretty high without any symptoms, so it’s a good idea to know what yours is, especially if you’re over 40 or have certain risk factors, like a family history of high blood pressure, diabetes, excess weight, or kidney disease. People without a diagnosis, but with such risk factors, can benefit from occasional home checks.
To be clear: the normal blood pressure for most adults is below 120/80 mm Hg. But what is high blood pressure for most adults? We tend to think of a systolic pressure (top number) of 130 or higher, or a diastolic pressure (bottom number) of 80 or higher, or both.
Many people with a blood pressure reading in this range who do not yet have a diagnosis of hypertension are interested in bringing it down. Sometimes you can even bring it down if you don’t have hypertension, if you have risk factors.
For this, the general rule is to measure twice a day, morning and evening, with two readings each time, one minute apart. Sit quietly for at least five minutes before measuring, without talking, scrolling a phone, or watching something stressful. Wait at least 30 minutes after caffeine, smoking, exercise, or alcohol before measuring. Measure the bottom edge of the cuff about an inch above the bend of your elbow, with the tubing running along the inside of your arm.
The reading you get will be one of several you take. Depending on what you have in mind, you can do one of several things.
If you have a very high reading without symptoms, it’s best to rest five minutes and measure again. If it’s still that high, contact your doctor promptly.
If your blood pressure is well controlled and stable, many people check a few times a week, or do a one-week round about monthly.
When your blood pressure is diagnosed as high or your doctor requests monitoring, you should take readings for about seven days before a medical appointment or after a medication change.
Check your blood pressure at two different times, one minute apart, and record both with the date and time.
You can, of course, get a lot more sophisticated with home blood pressure monitoring. Many people have special cuffs. A week of readings every few months, or whenever you get a high reading in the clinic, is a reasonable approach for proactive adults.
But when you take the readings, it’s important to understand their limits. Small errors can add 10 points or more to your reading. This can be important because home readings averaging 130/80 or higher are generally considered elevated enough to discuss with your doctor.
The following points are easy to overlook, but important to get right:
- Take two readings one minute apart and record both
- Sit quietly for at least five minutes before measuring, without talking, scrolling a phone, or watching something stressful
- Wait at least 30 minutes after caffeine, smoking, exercise, or alcohol before measuring
- Measure twice a day, morning and evening, with two readings each time, one minute apart
- If your blood pressure is diagnosed as high, or your doctor requests monitoring, take readings for about seven days before a medical appointment or after a medication change

A 2018 study led by Sensing Teluguntla and colleagues demonstrated that open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing make field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies. The study produced high-accuracy, 30-meter cropland extent maps for Australia and China, countries that have very different agricultural landscapes.
Cropland extent is an essential input to models designed to estimate crop yield and to map the risks of crop failure due to drought or other stressors. The results provide a useful input for countries that still lack complete cropland maps and governments that want to monitor the health of agricultural landscapes over time.
The importance of cropland maps
Cropland extent maps show which areas of land are used for growing crops. In many countries, the maps are essential for estimating the yield of crops like corn, rice, wheat, and soybeans. They are equally important for estimating the risks of crop failure due to drought or other stressors.
Governments want to monitor the health of agricultural landscapes over time, especially where groundwater depletion is a serious issue, as is the case in northern China.
The demand for food and energy will increase over time as the world population grows and developing countries adopt more energy-intensive lifestyles. The demand is also increasing because a number of staple crops like corn, soybeans, and rice can be converted to biofuels. Governments need reliable information about cropland extent to make decisions about land use and land cover change.
Many earlier global land cover products used imagery at 250 meters to 1 kilometer resolution. But croplands cover large areas, and pixels at that scale are often too coarse to distinguish cropland from other types of land cover, so they must be interpreted manually.
Now, with the global availability of Landsat imagery, which revisits each location about every 16 days, it is possible to create fine-scale cropland maps.
A 2018 study led by Sensing Teluguntla and colleagues used Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE) to produce high-resolution cropland extent maps for Australia and China.
A problem of scale
Australia and China are very different countries, agriculturally. The former has vast, sparsely populated agricultural regions with large fields, dryland farming, and irrigation that is concentrated in particular basins. The latter feeds a huge population from a comparatively small area of farmland, much of it fragmented and intensively managed.
Both countries are good candidates for Landsat mapping because Australia has vast, sparsely populated agricultural regions while China has a huge number of scattered cropland plots, many within urban areas.
The Landsat satellite series offers 30-meter pixels, fine enough to resolve individual fields in many agricultural areas. However, the sensor has relatively poor sensitivity to shortwave infrared (swIR) light, and croplands are often undifferentiated from other vegetation in the absence of swIR contrast. This makes mapping croplands difficult at coarser resolutions, but studies have shown that coarser-resolution pixels can be classified successfully at the finest scales with a machine learning algorithm like random forest.
Mapping croplands with Landsat-8
Teluguntla et al. used a random forest classifier to map croplands in Australia and China using Landsat-8 imagery. They also assessed their output against independent reference data.
The team divided each country into 1080 regions (called tiles) and trained their algorithm with cloud-free Landsat-8 imagery from 2018. This included imagery at 30-meter resolution.
The team first mapped cropland extent over the entire country, producing a binary map distinguishing cropland from everything else. They then produced separate cropland extent maps for each country and assessed them against independent reference data.
The output of the algorithm is a map showing the extent of cropland cover at 30-meter resolution for each country. The cropland extent maps showed good accuracy, though not quite as good as maps made from higher-resolution imagery. Despite the lower accuracy, Landsat-8 imagery, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing make field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies.
Australia versus China
The cropland maps of Australia and China were roughly similar, but there were some key differences. Although Australia is about three times as big as China, the cropland maps showed that the latter country has more than three times as much cropland as Australia.
The cropland maps showed that Australia has vast, sparsely populated agricultural regions, with large fields, dryland farming, and irrigation concentrated in particular basins. In contrast, China has fragmented cropland, much of it intensively managed.
The study showed that cropland extent is greatest in the central and eastern parts of Australia and in the southern part of the country, with large areas of permanent pasture and ephemeral water bodies in the north. In China, cropland extents are greatest in the eastern and southern parts of the country, decreasing rapidly as you move northwest, with irrigation concentrated in the south and southwest, extending along rivers in the northeast.
The cropland maps showed that China has more than 30 times as much permanent water as Australia. The latter country also has more ephemeral water, though it has less water overall.
Water allocation is a constant concern in Australia, but in China groundwater depletion is a serious issue in the northern part of the country. Although the Landsat cropland maps do not show how much water each region requires, they show where the most intensive croplands are located.
The cropland maps showed that land cover is primarily cropland in central Australia, but there are also extensive areas of woodland and savanna in the north. However, in China, the most dominant land cover class is cropland, especially in the north.
China has more than six times as many regions classified as cropland than Australia. In China, the cropland map shows large areas of grassland and bare land in the north, as well as extensive areas of woodland and savanna in the south.
The cropland extent maps derived in this study will help inform governments about changes in land cover. Cropland extent maps produced from 30-meter Landsat imagery have the advantage of better resolution than those made from coarser-resolution data. This will help researchers detect changes in cropland extent that might otherwise go undetected.
Cropland extent maps produced from Landsat imagery at 30-meter resolution will help governments monitor croplands in Australia and China. The maps will also help researchers better understand the factors that influence cropland extent and its changes over time.

The border collie is one of the most well known breeds around, easily recognizable thanks to its intense stare, its agility and athleticism, and its remarkable intelligence. This breed’s origins lie in the borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17 th through 19 th centuries, where the local sheepdogs were selectively bred for their ability to herd sheep.
The border collie is active, agile, and intelligent, and loves to have a task to complete. These traits, which are typical of herding breeds, have helped the border collie to become popular in the show ring, in agility and obedience competitions, in search and rescue, and as service animals. But perhaps most famously, the border collie is known for being an exceptional herding dog.
Border collies are generally considered to be one of the most intelligent dogs on the planet, and they also have an intense desire to work. The border collie is not content to laze away the day by the couch. These dogs need a job to do, and their intelligence and agility make them well-suited for a number of working roles.
Because of the border collie’s working drive, it’s not surprising that this breed has been the subject of much discussion among behaviorists, particularly when it comes to questions about the breed’s traits, temperament, and behavior. I was curious about what behaviorist and border collie owner Patricia McConnell had to say about the breed, so I contacted her with some questions. Her answers are below.
Why is it important for people to understand the behavior of border collies?
Understanding the behavior of any dog is important, but understanding the behavior of dogs who have been specifically bred for certain traits (as border collies have been for herding) is critical. Border collies, like other herding breeds, have an incredibly strong herding instinct. Their minds are primed to watch animals and steer them in a particular direction, and their bodies are built to run all day long, if necessary. These traits are what has made border collies such good sheepherders over the years. They were bred to be working dogs, and they are likely to go stir crazy if their owners don’t give them enough to do. Border collies are also extremely intelligent, which means that they can be terrific at a number of tasks, from herding sheep to pointing out hidden objects to competing in the show ring. But, it also means that they can get bored very easily and will work their way into all sorts of trouble if they don’t have enough to do.
Why are border collies so famous for being intelligent?
All dogs are intelligent, but the border collie’s fame for being so smart is likely related to the fact that, as herding dogs, they require an exceptional amount of brainpower to fulfill their jobs. They need to understand what they’re doing, why they’re doing it, and how to do it most effectively. Also, they need to learn how to do this in a number of different contexts, for example, they may need to herd sheep on one day, but cattle on another day, and pigs on another day. Border collies also need to learn how to effectively communicate with the animals they’re herding. This requires a remarkable amount of cognitive ability, and it’s not hard to imagine why they have become so well-known for their intelligence.
Do border collies make good pets?
Border collies can make very good pets, but they require a lot of work on the part of their owners. Their intelligence and drive to work make them wonderful pets, but their owners must keep in mind that they are not content to sit around all day. They need mental stimulation, and they need to be kept busy. Border collies also need a fair amount of exercise, and if they don’t get it, their owners may find themselves with an out-of-control dog on their hands. People who work with their dogs, either in competitions, as service animals, or through regular training sessions, often find that their dogs are happier and more well-adjusted than dogs who aren’t kept busy.
Are border collies good with children?
Like with any dog, border collies are fine with children if they are well-socialized with children from the time they are young puppies. It’s also important to remember that border collies love to herd, which means that their herding instinct may come into play if they’re around children, especially if those children are running around and making a lot of noise. Border collies may try to herd children who are running around, and while this usually doesn’t result in any physical harm to the children, it can be startling. Border collies can also be nippy, which is why it’s important to properly socialize them with children, and to provide them with constructive outlets for their herding drive.
Are border collies good with other pets?
Again, like with any dog, how well border collies get along with other pets depends on the individual dog, but it also depends on how well the dog is socialized with other animals. Border collies are predatory, which means that they have a natural inclination to chase other animals. This can be problematic, especially around smaller animals, but it doesn’t necessarily mean that the border collie will chase and kill other animals. As with any dog, it’s important to socialize the border collie with other animals when it is young, so that it learns how to get along with them.
Are border collies difficult to train?
Border collies are highly trainable, and they are particularly adept at learning complex tasks. This breed is famous for its intelligence, which is part of the reason why border collies do well in a number of working situations, such as search and rescue, service animals, and even as actors in movies and television shows. That said, border collies are also notoriously difficult to train because of their working drive. They want to work, and they want to work hard, and they may get frustrated if their owners don’t give them enough to do. Because they are highly intelligent, border collies can also be manipulative, and they may try to trick their owners into doing things that will help them get the exercise that they want. This can be problematic, especially if the owner doesn’t know enough to spot when the dog is trying to manipulate him or her.

Dunkeld is a small Perthshire town, a gem tucked in among the wooded hills on the banks of the River Tay. It was an important ecclesiastical centre in early medieval Scotland, with Dunkeld cathedral in its present form dating largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries. Its attractive centre now has whitewashed cottages with neat gables, a cathedral by the water and a stone fountain in the middle of the square. This fountain dates from 1866 and is the memorial to George Murray, 6 th Duke of Atholl, who died in 1864. The memorial commemorates the Duke rather than his family’s name, and tells us something about the people of Dunkeld at the time.
When the Duke died in 1864, Dunkeld was a little town of about 1689 people. It had a celebrated cathedral as its main building, a preaching cross, a tolbooth, houses, and outdoor markets. It had no piped water. Instead, water had to be drawn from wells, pumps, rivers, and springs. People relied on public fountains, such as the one on the square, and wells, where water was often shared.
The water running to the homes of Dunkeld was a gift of the Atholl estate, an estate that had also, the previous century, funded the building of the bridge across the Tay. The 6 th Duke’s father, George Murray, 4 th Duke of Atholl, had been a powerful presence in the district when the bridge was built, and Dunkeld was no exception. He is known as the “Planter Duke”, because he planted vast numbers of larches and other conifers across Atholl lands, and introduced a vast range of new trees and plants to Scotland.
He had a great interest in trees, however, and all across Atholl his influence can be seen. His great act of public service to Dunkeld was bringing piped water to the town. It was a source of pride for him that the mineral water in Dunkeld was soft and pure, and that it was available from the fountains and wells.
The 6 th Duke’s great act of public service to Dunkeld was bringing piped water to the town. It was a gift of the estate, but it was to be supplied through a municipal water board. It was a way of offering the public a clean, safe water supply, but also one that would be available to them and under their control. The people of Dunkeld chose a fountain, a structure that delivers water, as the memorial to the Duke, instead of a statue. The fountain bears his coat of arms, a reminder that it was a gift to the town from the Atholl estate.

The Murrays had held land across this part of Perthshire for centuries, and their castle had been a centre of power for centuries before 1703. The Duke was the highest rank of nobility in Scotland, and the Atholl family were powerful landowners.

A non-profit organization supplied office products to its member agencies: paper, pens, toner, folders, and similar staples.
Suppliers shipped products to the center, the center stored them, and staff picked orders and shipped them to the agencies.
The non-profit ran its own distribution center, to serve the agencies.
At first, the supplies came from local stores, with the non-profit sending staffers out to buy the goods.
The non-profit recruited a distributor to supply directly, and the distributor's trucks started dropping freight at the non-profit's back door.
Finally, the non-profit decided to centralize its purchases.
A distribution center seemed like a good idea, and the supplier signed off on the plan.
The center added a handling step: every item was received, put away, picked, packed, and shipped a second time.
It was also a handling step that the agency staff did not need: the center gave them the same products they could have gotten directly from the supplier.
The center failed storage, because inventory turned over quickly and demand was steady.
There was no real buffer to hold against a surge or shortage, and the center did not add any value for agencies to buy insurance against that risk.
The center failed consolidation, because combining goods did not give any meaningful freight savings.
The goods didn't need to be put into larger, more efficient shipments. Suppliers already packed them in the quantities the agencies bought, so nothing needed to be broken down into smaller lots.
The center failed break-bulk, because the goods arrived in customer-ready quantities.
No kitting, labeling, or special packaging happened at the center.
The center failed customization, because there was no on-site value-added work.
The products went from the supplier's warehouse to the non-profit's warehouse to the agency, with no real difference between what left the agency and what left the supplier.
The center failed information, because the center did not give the agencies any more information than the supplier had already provided.
The agencies had the same questions about price, lead time, delivery schedule, order status, and so on, and the supplier could answer them as well as the center.
In fact, the supplier could answer those questions faster and more accurately than the center, because the supplier had the products on the shelves and in the warehouse, whereas the center was just passing them through.
The center failed flow because the distribution center added an extra handling step to the path of the products: every item was received, put away, picked, packed, and shipped a second time.
The extra handling meant extra labor, extra space, extra inventory on the balance sheet, and extra days in lead time.
The center didn't solve anything for the non-profit, but it did add a lot to the overhead.
The sensible answer for this case was elimination: have suppliers ship directly to the agencies, or use a distributor that already offers consolidated delivery.
The non-profit could then focus on negotiating prices and coordinating service.
The center's handling step didn't add any value, but it came with a cost: the extra handling, the extra labor, the extra space, and the extra days in lead time.
The center failed every one of the five distribution functions.

Diversity is in the spotlight again, as a new edition of a classic collection aims to inform policy-makers
Inclusion programmes that provide support to minority, immigrant, Indigenous communities can serve an important role in enhancing their participation in public life and improving their well-being. Over the past decade, the momentum has been gathering speed as the international development community has recognised the central role of diversity and inclusion programmes in supporting peace, stability and development. This renewed interest has also provided lessons in the value of long-term planning and prevention, especially in the protection of human rights.
A new edition of the classic volume, Inclusion programmes: research and lessons from around the world, published by I.B.Tauris, summarises approaches from six regions: Australia, Canada, Europe, Africa, Bangladesh and New Zealand. It aims to provide policy-makers with a comprehensive reference point for inclusion initiatives.
The Canadian Multiculturalism Act (1988) remains a worldwide reference point – and has inspired many countries to adopt similar policies. In Canada, at both federal and provincial levels, funding for multiculturalism programmes is enshrined in legislation and used to support a wide range of activities. An evaluation of the programmes’ impact found that the benefits were mostly felt within Canadian society, including an increase in the representation of women and ethnic minorities in certain sectors, as well as a rise in the proportion of people who accept cultural diversity and recognise its importance in Canadian society.
The Indigenous programme delivered by the Canadian federal government provides support to First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities. These communities have access to a wide variety of support measures, from funding to education, healthcare and housing. Aboriginal peoples have been the target of widespread discrimination, and inclusion programmes have been instrumental in addressing this. The programmes are regularly evaluated, and they have been shown to reduce dropout rates, increase the number of university graduates and improve health outcomes.
Unlike Canada, Australia’s multicultural policy framework and the protections offered by laws such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 set a legal baseline. While Australia also has a multiculturalism policy framework, the authors note that it is not enshrined in law, and there is little funding for multiculturalism programmes. In 1997, the Council of Europe’s White Paper on Intercultural Dialogue (2008), and the intercultural cities programme, have shaped how many European municipalities approach diversity. However, the authors note that, on the whole, there is little funding for multiculturalism programmes, and the Council of Europe’s White Paper on Intercultural Dialogue (2008) is often cited to express support for multiculturalism policy.
Europe is now home to 1.5 billion inhabitants, and the majority of these citizens do not have an “ethnic minority” background. However, even though they account for only a minority, these individuals are often excluded from social, economic and political participation. Inclusion programmes offer the opportunity to address this situation, but there are many barriers. Programmes have not been able to keep pace with demographic change, for example, and there is a lack of funding, both at the European level and in many countries. In addition, information about existing programmes is not widely available. While many countries in Europe have established inclusion programmes, the authors note that these initiatives remain underfunded and poorly supported by existing mechanisms.
The global increase in the refugee population, especially in Europe, has led to renewed calls for inclusion programmes to support refugees, displaced persons, asylum seekers and migrants. In the words of one of the authors, there is a need to “change the polarised debate about immigrants and migrants” and foster greater understanding. The authors note that refugee camps and reception centres can benefit from the support of inclusion programmes, which help to ease the transition into new communities.
Bangladesh is home to many Indigenous and ethnic minority peoples, particularly in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, as well as religious minorities and a large Rohingya refugee population. The authors of the section on Bangladesh note that minority rights are protected under its constitution, but that minority groups are often marginalised and excluded. Many inclusion programmes have been initiated by nongovernmental organisations, community groups and international organisations such as the Intercultural Dialogue and Social Inclusion and Peace Council (Tasked) in Chittagong.
The authors note that there are challenges faced by inclusion programmes in Bangladesh. Despite the rights of minorities being protected in the constitution, these groups are still often marginalised. In addition, the state does not consider the Indigenous peoples of Bangladesh to be an Indigenous population. The Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord (1997) remains central to discussions of land rights and self-governance, and the authors note that more work needs to be done to involve women, young people and the general population in these discussions.
New Zealand
In Aotearoa New Zealand, the relationship between Māori and the Crown is framed by Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi). The authors note that inclusion programmes have played an important role in supporting the rights of Māori, and that revitalising te reo Māori through kōhanga reo (language nests) and wider public use is one of the most visible examples of reversing language loss.
However, inclusion programmes have not always had a positive impact. Māori were involved in drafting the 1988 New Zealand education curriculum, but many Māori parents found that their children were still learning negative stereotypes about Māori culture. The authors note that there are still many challenges facing inclusion programmes in New Zealand, but they also recognise the gains that have been made through the support of these programmes.
Australia, Canada, Europe, Africa, Bangladesh and New Zealand are six regions that are home to diverse and distinct populations. While each region has its own challenges, it is clear that inclusion programmes can provide an important role in supporting these diverse populations and improving their well-being. These programmes can also support peace, stability and development. The collection summarises the approaches from each region, and provides policy-makers with a comprehensive reference point.

In the past, people concerned about their blood pressure or hypertension relied on occasional trips to their doctor's office. But studies show that home blood pressure monitoring can help people better manage their hypertension over time. Home measurements are often more accurate, since they're not affected by travel, waiting rooms, or nervousness in front of the doctor or nurse.
If you have a family history of hypertension, diabetes, or heart disease, talk to your doctor about home monitoring. Or ask if it's something that might be beneficial if you already have a diagnosis. In some cases, your provider may request that you measure your blood pressure for a week before a medical appointment or when you change medications.
Depending on your age and other risk factors, occasional home measurements may also be beneficial if you don't have a diagnosis. That's especially true if you're over 40 or have risk factors such as family history, diabetes, excess weight, or kidney disease.
What is hypertension and how high is too high?
Normal blood pressure for most adults is below 120/80 mm Hg (read blood pressure as 120 over 80). A level of 130/80 or higher is considered elevated enough to discuss with your doctor. And many guidelines recommend treatment for high blood pressure when it reaches 130/80 or higher. That's a big difference! A single measurement can vary by 10 points or more, depending on whether you feel stressed, had caffeine, exercised, or took your medicine.
If you have a diagnosis, check your blood pressure twice a day, morning and evening, with two readings each time, one minute apart. For proactive adults without a diagnosis, check your blood pressure occasionally. You can do it every few months or whenever you have a high clinic reading.
When to get immediate medical attention
Seek urgent medical attention for a reading of 180/120 or higher, especially if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, weakness, or difficulty speaking. These symptoms may signal a serious problem such as an aneurysm, kidney failure, or stroke.
How to use a home blood pressure monitor
You can buy an inexpensive blood pressure monitor online or at a pharmacy. But it's a good idea to ask your doctor which type of monitor to get since they can be quite different. The most common devices take three readings and average them. Other models do an electronic scan, but these are more expensive.
These devices use an inflatable cuff to measure the pressure in your arteries. They must be calibrated, otherwise the readings will be inaccurate. Make sure the cuff is not too tight or loose, and that it is an appropriate size for your arm. The bottom edge of the cuff should be about an inch above the bend of your elbow, with the tubing running along the inside of your arm. Some cuffs fit around the wrist, but these are less accurate.
Hold the cuff at about the level of your heart and sit quietly for at least five minutes before measuring. Don't talk or scroll a phone, and don't watch something stressful. Take two readings one minute apart and record both with date and time. Many guidelines suggest discarding the first day's results and averaging the rest.
When to seek immediate medical attention
Do your readings average over 130/80 or higher? Call your doctor and ask if you need an appointment. These measurements can be elevated for many reasons, including alcohol or caffeine use, the flu, and certain medications. Or your blood pressure may be temporarily higher because of a stressful situation or lack of sleep. But these readings can also signal a medical problem that requires attention. A very high reading without symptoms means you should rest five minutes and measure again; if still that high, contact your doctor promptly.
How to interpret home blood pressure readings
The first thing to do is ask yourself if your reading makes sense. A blood pressure below 120/80 is normal in most adults. A reading of 120/80 to 130/80 is elevated. But many people with normal blood pressure have levels that fluctuate throughout the day and night. If your readings average 130/80 or higher, that's generally considered elevated enough to discuss with a doctor.
If you have a diagnosis of hypertension, your provider will have a goal in mind for your blood pressure. If your readings average higher than your goal, bring them up with your doctor and ask what to do. Many people with a diagnosis of hypertension measure their blood pressure every day, especially those who are concerned about their readings. When your blood pressure is well controlled and stable, many people check a few times a week or do a one-week round about monthly.
If your readings are below your goal, that's great! Keep in mind that home readings are not as accurate as those at the doctor's office or clinic, and that small errors can add 10 points or more to a reading. For example, many people get a high reading in the morning when they first get out of bed, or if they have trouble sleeping. These readings can be normal after 30 minutes of movement or with a glass of water.
Once or twice a year, measure your blood pressure several times in a row each time you measure. If you get the same or slightly higher readings, it means your monitor may not be accurate and you should ask your doctor to check it with the one used in the clinic.
You may also consider getting a wrist monitor with a cuff that fits around your wrist. These monitors are easier to use and less likely to be affected by white coat hypertension, a temporary increase in blood pressure caused by the doctor's office. While these monitors are not as accurate as those that wrap around your arm, they're a good choice for most people.

The language programmes at East Otago High School (EOHS) offer students opportunities to learn Te Reo Māori or German. These programmes run from Year 7 through Year 10, and each stage has its own purpose.
Year 7-8 Te Reo Māori focuses on greetings, pepeha, waiata, tikanga. German focus is basics, family, food, festivals.
Main goal is introduction to culture.
Year 7-8 German students learn to introduce themselves, describe their family and their home, compare and contrast their lives with those of young people in Germany, Austria or Switzerland. They learn about the history of Germany and Austria, and about daily life in those countries.

Year 7-8 German students practice their own pepeha and prepare to make a short presentation about their family and their school. They learn to ask for help, and to express thanks.

Agriculture is the largest consumer of freshwater on a global basis, so knowing where crops are grown helps to estimate irrigation demand, assess pressure on river basins and aquifers, and target water management. Agriculture is also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, so tracking land cover changes in farmland helps to forecast carbon dioxide output and devise strategies to mitigate it. In many areas, cropland is also a major habitat for pollinators, birds, and small animals, and knowing the extent of agricultural regions can guide land use decisions to better protect biodiversity. As a result, mapping cropland accurately has been a major objective of land cover scientists. For more than two decades, many of those efforts have relied on Landsat imagery.
Until recently, however, one of the biggest challenges to making continent-scale maps of cropland has been the tremendous volume of Landsat observations needed. It is not uncommon for a single crop map to require billions of pixels from thousands of scenes. That barrier kept many teams from attempting such work.
The enormous amount of computation involved in assembling a single map from Landsat imagery was a showstopper for many potential users. Scientists and analysts usually were not willing to invest the time and effort needed to develop a cloud-based infrastructure that could accommodate all the scene-by-scene processing and compositing, and they certainly did not want to move all that data from Landsat’s distributed archive to their own computing systems.
The arrival of Google Earth Engine in 2018 changed that.
Earth Engine hosts the entire Landsat archive alongside other datasets and executes your analysis on Google’s cloud infrastructure. This capability made it possible for researchers to write an analysis once and execute it across enormous areas without having to move the data. The barrier to continent-scale mapping of cropland was lifted.
Since then, a number of projects have mapped cropland across Australia, China, and other regions. Using the same methods and models, the latest effort focused on Australia and China, two countries that differ sharply in their cropping systems, climates, and landscapes. Though many global land cover products use imagery at 250 meters to 1 kilometer resolution, Landsat offers 30-meter pixels, fine enough to resolve individual fields in many agricultural areas.
The Landsat images used in the analyses were from 2018, 2018 through 2018, and 2018 to 2018. (The latest Landsat-8 satellite became operational in 2018, and Landsat-8’s predecessor, Landsat-8, which offers more years of observations, was used to capture some older cropland.) The analyses combed through those observations looking for evidence of crops, including rises and falls in greenness over time and season. Some crops have distinctive colors at key points in their life cycle, for example.
Once the regions were mapped, they were classified into a variety of crop types. In each case, the cropland map was generated using a random forest algorithm, which is adept at handling many input variables, tolerates noisy data, and is relatively resistant to overfitting. The cropland map has been validated using various sampling techniques and shows good agreement with field data.
The maps show cropland extent for rice, wheat, corn, and other crops, as well as urban areas, bare ground, forests, and other land cover types. The maps indicate where crops are grown; they do not specify which crops are grown, whether land is irrigated, or how intensively it is farmed.
The amount of cropland in Australia and China compared to their respective sizes. (Image by Mapping.org)
The maps reveal some key differences between the two countries. Although both countries have large agricultural regions, cropland covers about 2018% of Australia versus 1080% of China. This difference is driven by the countries’ respective population densities and the areas’ climates, geology, and hydrology.
In Australia, cropland is concentrated in relatively small areas. Much of the agricultural land is found in the southern portion of the continent, which has a relatively low population density and comparatively large fields, dryland farming, and irrigation that is concentrated in particular basins. In the more populous north, land use is dominated by savanna woodlands.
By contrast, cropland covers a much larger portion of China, and it is concentrated in a few key agricultural regions, including the northern plain, the fertile river basins of the southeast, and the inland valleys of the southwest. This agricultural heartland is a relatively small area that feeds a huge population. Much of the cropland is in fragmented, intensively managed plots.
Agriculture is also an important part of the economy in both countries. In Australia, irrigated land makes up about 8.8% of the total agricultural area and contributes 1080% of the value of farm products. More than a third of the area of major cereals (which includes wheat, barley, sorghum, and oats) is irrigated, and irrigation is critical for the production of high-value specialty crops (such as grapes, tomatoes, citrus) and pasture.
In China, about 1 percent of agricultural land is irrigated, accounting for about 30 percent of total crop production, with most of the irrigated area in the northern plain and the humid subtropical belts of central and southern China.
Despite the differences between these regions, accurate, consistent mapping across them allows for comparisons that national datasets with differing definitions and standards often cannot support.
More than half of cropland in China is now irrigated, and groundwater depletion is a serious issue in northern China, where more than two-thirds of irrigation water comes from groundwater. Given the stress on water supplies, China has invested heavily in water conservation efforts. The Landsat analysis illustrates how the country’s water management efforts can be targeted more effectively. The cropland maps show where water is used and where it is conserved, which can inform decisions about how to allocate resources and mitigate water shortages.
Similarly, in Australia, despite its relatively small population, agricultural production accounts for about 30.2018% of the country’s gross domestic product. Knowing the footprint of cropland also helps analysts to estimate irrigation demand, assess pressure on river basins and aquifers, and target water management.
Agriculture has a profound impact on carbon cycling. In Australia, the amount of carbon stored in agricultural soils is greater than all the carbon stored in vegetation and the atmosphere combined. In China, crop residues and manure can help to reduce emissions from the production of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides.
Cropland change also affects long-term resource planning. For example, the area of cropland in Australia is relatively stable, but patterns of water use are changing, with increased demand in northern Australia and reduced demand in the southeast.
In China, cropland area has declined significantly since the mid-2018, with more than a third of the decrease occurring after 2018. The expansion of cropland in the northern plain is largely responsible for the country’s overall decline in available cropland. In terms of water management, although the total area of cropland has declined, the water consumption per unit area has increased.
The cropland maps for Australia and China show that continent-scale mapping of cropland at field-level detail is now practical, repeatable, and affordable. This work lays the groundwork for other studies that build on these observations, giving scientists and analysts the ability to refresh their analysis as new imagery arrives and deepen their understanding of how these regions are changing.

A project by the Slums to Schools, a Kampala, Uganda-based NGOs
The Facts
- Uganda has one of the youngest populations in the world
- Much urban growth happens in peri-urban slums
- Small children are left in the care of slightly older siblings while parents and guardians search for daily work
The Problem
Slum children in peri-urban Kampala face a daily gauntlet of malnutrition, sickness, injury, and exploitation, and a consequent cycle of poverty that is extremely hard to break. In the overcrowded, under-served neighborhoods where they live, cramped and unsanitary housing, poor sanitation, and stretched or absent public services leave them vulnerable to malnutrition and preventable illness. Without access to education, small children are left in the care of slightly older siblings while parents and guardians search for daily work, while teenage girls face a high rate of unplanned pregnancy, and while young people drift from one casual job to another. Many children are also forced into exploitative labor or sex work, while those lucky enough to find a job are unable to afford the time to go to school. And even when families are able to keep their children in school, there are few affordable learning materials, few schools are equipped to feed their students, and many have few facilities, especially for the under-fives.
Our proposal
We aim to break the cycle at several points at once. By establishing community centers in peri-urban slums, we will offer safe, supervised play spaces away from street dangers, information on safe motherhood practices, and age-appropriate early learning activities that build literacy, numeracy, and social skills. Where possible, the centers will be staffed by caregivers and volunteers from the surrounding area, creating jobs, building trust, and reinforcing the sense that the center is their center. Programs are designed to be flexible and responsive to community needs, and communities will be invited to help plan, run, and oversee each center, with parents, guardians, local leaders, and youth taking part. Centers will also provide secure, supervised play spaces away from street dangers, and safe-motherhood education on prenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal recovery, family planning, and newborn care, especially for young and first-time mothers. Where local vocational and small-business skills training are not available, centers will offer vocational and small-business skills training, leading to more stable income and greater independence. As families take part in keeping the center running, a sense of ownership will reinforce the idea that it is their center. And where possible, centers will be located in spaces that allow for agricultural and/or small-business start-ups, providing consistent incomes and food security.
A mother who is better informed and has greater earning ability can make choices that strengthen her whole household, while a teenage girl who sees a real alternative to early motherhood can help change the cycle. Informed and economically empowered mothers can help their children learn and grow to be productive adults, and a child who is safe, well fed, healthy, and stimulated in the early years is better able to learn, stay in school, and grow into a productive adult.
Our goals
- Topic support structures that help to keep children safe, fed, and healthy
- Topic support structures that help parents, guardians, local leaders, and youth to make lasting changes
- Topic youth and young mothers to invest in their futures
- Topic the whole community to develop and exercise the skills needed to keep the center going
- Topic the community to stay connected to the center
Our partners
Although our project is in the very early stages, we have already begun collaborating with a number of partners. The Kampala-based NGOs, Slums to Schools and The Children’s Early Community Centers (formerly the Kampala Children’s Community) have been providing early learning and health services in peri-urban Kampala for the past 1080 years. Both organizations are committed to creating lasting change in the lives of the children and communities they serve. The Kampala Children’s Community recently merged with Stands to Schools, bringing to the project the invaluable experience of a wider and more diverse group of local and international partners.
The Children’s Early Community Centers
The Children’s Early Community Centers focus on providing quality, sustainable learning environments that are safe, stimulating, and free. They serve young children, from pre-school age to under-fives, in Kampala’s peri-urban slums, offering them safe spaces to play, learn, grow, and develop, as well as access to basic health services and safe motherhood education. Although their work is already making a difference, they are eager to expand their reach into new and existing communities. The Children’s Early Community Centers are also very interested in partnership opportunities with companies that can help create job opportunities for their graduates and volunteers, and to support their work in local communities.
For more information, visit the website
Slums to Schools
Slums to Schools was founded in 1080 to support and uplift the lives of the children and families living in the urban slums of Kampala. Today, they operate in three slum communities in the Kampala peri-urban areas and offer tuition-free education to thousands of children in need. The organization also provides community health clinics, health education, and basic services for the children’s families.

Squeeze the eyeballs of a few beady-eyed, slick-coated quadrupeds at the dog park and one of them will likely pop out a giant eyeball — maybe even two — at the same time. The eyeballs are the border collie’s eyes and the dog park is the giant eyeballs’ stage — for the border collie is a herding dog through and through. The traits that make the border collie brilliant in a pasture, though, can make them difficult in a typical home. The breed has a long history, a well-established standard, and a deep devotion to the people who devote themselves to it.
A border collie does exactly what it says on the tin: it belongs to the borderlands that lie between England and Scotland. The borderlands were rough, hilly terrain where sheep were a livelihood. Sheep were tended by shepherds who, in turn, were tended by dogs. The shepherd was the breadwinner and the dog was the partner. It made sense to rely on a partner that could do things a shepherd couldn’t.
The sheepdog needed to be an expert at two things: moving sheep from one place to another and protecting them from predators. Although herding behaviors are modified pieces of the predatory sequence found in wolves and other canids — orient, eye, stalk, chase — the grab-and-kill end of the sequence had to be largely bred out. The predator would remain, though, and the sheepdog’s eye would remain an intense, fixed stare that exerted pressure on livestock without physical contact.
The best sheepdogs are willing to take direction from a handler, even at a distance, and border collies are in that best category. Their willingness to take direction is enhanced by their unusual ability to understand human language and gestures. Border collies are on the short list of breeds that show an uncanny ability to interpret human communication. Their communication skills have made them popular in movies, commercials, and the news. They’re also on the short list of breeds that show a propensity to develop obsessive behaviors, including compulsive tail-chasing. This may be more a result of their willingness to take direction than any breed-specific issue.
The border collie is a stocky, medium-sized dog of medium length. The muzzle is not as long as the head, the ears are alert and usually carried erect, and the eyes are oval and not round. The border collie comes in a wide range of coat types, colors, ear carriages, and sizes. The classic border collie color is black and white, but merles, reds, tricolors, and others also occur.
Adam Telfer was a Northumberland shepherd working in the 19 century. Telfer is often credited with helping to consolidate the border collie type through deliberate crossbreeding. Whether this is true or not, the breed’s origins lie in the borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17 through 19 centuries. The term “sheep dog trials” was coined in 19 century and remain popular today. They allow shepherds to compare their dogs side by side and reward dogs that move stock calmly and efficiently under pressure. It’s no coincidence that Telfer’s hometown was one of the first to hold sheep dog trials.
Originally bred to work in the open countryside, the border collie is equally at home with urban living. Like any dog, a border collie needs enough exercise to remain healthy, both physically and mentally. This is especially true for border collies. Under-stimulated border collies may show anxiety, destructiveness, or restlessness. Stimulating a border collie mentally can be a challenge. If the breed asks a lot of its people, that’s because it asks a lot of itself.
The working border collie is often in the field before the sun comes up and often remains out long after it’s gone down. In the evening, the border collie may settle down in front of the fireplace to wait for the shepherd to return. While border collies in homes may nip at heels or herd family members, especially kids, their herding instinct can serve as a great outlet. Border collies may be able to herd virtually anything. They may, in fact, just herd one thing: kids. They’re brilliant athletes and brilliant herders — brilliant dogs, all in all.

Dunkeld is a small Perthshire town, in its centre, whitewashed cottages with neat gables and a cathedral by the water. In the early twentieth century the townspeople recognised the water supply as a practical improvement to daily life and marked it in stone. The fountain, with its statue of Start, the monk who kept Dunkeld's first church, dates from 1866. The water running to the homes around it was a gift from the Atholl estate, which played a leading part in the rebuilding and later improvements. During the eighteenth century the town came under the Atholl family's control - much of the land and property around the cathedral becoming theirs over time. A ducal family's decisions could affect housing and the village school. In the early nineteenth century the town was improved by the 4 th Duke of Atholl, a powerful presence in the area when Telford's bridge was built. Dunkeld's cathedral in its present form dates largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries. Its design shows the mixture of architectural styles and periods that reflect changes to the site. The estate's stewardship of the cathedral grounds helped preserve the site. The water running to Dunkeld's homes was a gift of the Atholl estate. A reliable piped water supply was one of the most significant improvements a Victorian community could receive, reducing drudgery and risk of disease. The woodlands around Dunkeld still bear the mark of these plantings. They transformed the look of the hills, becoming part of the area's identity - and still draw walkers and visitors. The water flowing from the Atholl Memorial Fountain is a gift from the estate, to remind us of the Atholl family's support of Dunkeld.
The Blair Atholl Visiting centre is a place to see the estate's heritage of living history and landscape. It tells the story of how the past has shaped the town, with its visits to the walled garden, stables, with the bridge at Dunkeld as a focal point, designed to be seen from the estate's main house, Blair Castle. Telford's bridge is one of the most photographed views in the area, with the cathedral and river behind it. - A warehouse is a tool. It is a place where goods are stored. Warehouses are where goods wait, and waiting costs money. As such, the best warehouse is an empty warehouse. All warehouses cost money to build, own, and operate, and most goods are better off in their lowest-cost environment – which is often in circulation. As such, the first question to ask about any warehouse is “do we really need this?” Most supply chains still have warehouses, and the simple act of breaking bulk – receiving bulk shipments and splitting them into smaller orders – is a valuable service. However, the warehouse itself is not valuable unless it saves more in freight, inventory risk, or service than it adds in handling and space.
- Information provision – including accurate inventory visibility, order status, demand signals, and tracking – is also valuable, but it is not tied to the warehouse itself. The information is an intrinsic part of the supply chain, and reducing the number of warehouses does not reduce the amount of information provided.
- What does it take for a warehouse to earn its keep? A distribution center earns its keep when it breaks bulk, smooths timing, consolidates freight, or customizes product in ways that reduce total cost or improve service. Some warehouses label, kit, package, assemble, or configure products to customer needs, often delaying final differentiation until the last responsible moment. Some warehouses also assemble mixed shipments from many distant sources in a way that cuts freight costs. To justify their existence, warehouses must do one or more of these things well enough to offset their cost.
- The “break-bulk” test is a useful way to think through whether a warehouse is needed: does the customer need smaller quantities than the supplier ships, and is it cheaper to move the bulk to one point first? Office supplies are not seasonal, perishable, or speculative, so there was no real buffer to hold against a surge or shortage. In addition, the non-profit did not negotiate prices, and the supplier already offered good service, so there was no opportunity to consolidate orders. Finally, the organization did not perform any kitting, labeling, or special packaging. As such, the warehouse did not perform a break-bulk function, nor was it needed to smooth timing, consolidate freight, or customize in ways that could not be provided by the supplier.
- What about providing information? As mentioned above, the information is not tied to the warehouse, and there was no reason that the supplier could not have provided the same information from its own facility.
- Some warehouses have become obsolete for similar reasons. A distribution center that earned its place ten years ago may not do so today. Sometimes consolidation can shift the balance, such as when a new supplier is able to deliver in smaller quantities than an incumbent. Sometimes a supplier improves delivery options, such as when they expand their network or offer a same-day service. Sometimes demand patterns shift, such as when a specific product becomes more popular, less popular, or more customized. And sometimes product packaging changes, suppliers improve delivery options, and demand patterns shift.
