A new collection of country profiles highlights the power of co-designed governance, legislation, programs and policies to foster strong and equitable societies.
The collection, produced by the New Zealand Council for Civil Dialogue (Civic Dialogue) and the New Zealand Multiculturalism and Social Inclusion Council (Multiculturalism Council), summarises approaches from six regions — Australia, Canada, Europe, Africa, Bangladesh, New Zealand — for how to leverage the power of multiculturalism and inclusion to foster more positive, equitable, and peaceful societies.
The profiles are the fruit of a two-year co-design process led by the Multiculturalism Council’s Aotearoa New Zealand Civil Dialogue, in which Indigenous people’s organisations, civil society, local government, immigrant communities, and governments all participated.
The collection is intended to be a living resource for those looking to strengthen the effectiveness of their policies and programs on inclusion and multiculturalism. The collection touches on a range of issues, from bridging the divide between Indigenous self-determination and immigrant inclusion, to breaking down barriers between majority and minority communities, and to fostering more positive experiences of citizenship among newcomers.
In the table below, we’ve summarised key takeaways from the collection on how to advance inclusion and multiculturalism.
The table includes just a selection of takeaways, but you can read more at the collection’s new online platform.
Table of key takeaways
What’s the takeaway?
How is it being applied?
Demonstrate solidarity with Indigenous peoples and local ethnic communities
The National Dialogue in Bangladesh recognises and respects the cultural values of Indigenous peoples. This facilitates inter-ethnic relationships, particularly in areas of governance, education, healthcare, and resource development.
Legal frameworks for human rights and equality underpin inclusive governance
The Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord (1997) remains central to discussions of land rights and self-governance. By extending equal legal protection to Indigenous peoples, it provides a basis for further dialogue and cooperation.
Promote inclusive and effective public services
Local government in Aotearoa New Zealand is mandated to take cultural diversity into account when developing community policy, providing support to minority communities, and ensuring access to services. Indigenous languages are regularly used in council meetings, and Indigenous people are represented on council committees.
Citizen participation is key
Processes of co-creation can help to build trust between Indigenous communities and local governments. For example, the development of the 2008 Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord was a product of dialogue and consensus among Indigenous communities, and building on existing structures of community governance.
Land rights and self-determination need to be addressed together
The New Zealand Māori Council raises awareness of Māori values and aspirations for self-determination, and facilitates dialogue with government about economic development.
Local governments in Europe hold inclusive city-level diversity audits to examine who uses libraries, parks, and public services, and who does not. This helps to ensure that services are appropriate and accessible.
Community participation in public service delivery
The development and implementation of policies to protect Indigenous languages, such as te reo Māori in Aotearoa New Zealand, require community involvement at all stages.

Mother-tongue early education helps Indigenous children transition into school without losing their languages. Civic Dialogue in Aotearoa New Zealand developed recommendations for positive cultural interactions with education authorities, teachers, and students.

Pacific-led health and education initiatives build on community and church networks. They connect migrant communities to other settlement services, and ensure community members who work in health and education sectors feel supported.

Local governments around refugee settlements in Europe work with host communities to ease tension over scarce resources. This includes support for youth to establish their own non-governmental organisations, and establishing dialogue with parents’ associations.

The three numbers that count most are the first, the middle, and the last—blood pressure, body mass index (about weight), and blood sugar (about diabetes). Blood pressure naturally rises and falls throughout the day, so patterns matter more than individual readings. Consistent timing, rest, and correct sitting, right cuff size, and keeping records make a home device a tool for protecting your heart, brain, and kidneys.
All of the clinics and hospitals at Making, including the annual health-screening service for Making members, will measure your blood pressure with a reliable clinic device. Take-home reading often tells more about your individual situation, but it takes only a few minutes to reveal a risk factor years before it causes harm.
What’s normal?
Normal blood pressure for most adults is below 120/80 mm Hg. These numbers represent the pressure with each heartbeat, when the heart squeezes (systolic) and rests (diastolic), respectively. For most people, either too high or too low is unusual, but it happens. Older people and those with chronic illnesses sometimes have an abnormally low reading, and those with hypertension (high blood pressure) may have a very high reading.
Getting started
The device you choose should be reliable. The best types are those with an arm cuff (a watch or wrist monitor won’t do). Upper-arm automatic monitors are generally more accurate than wrist or finger devices. Setup errors can make a good device give misleading results, so use the manual or online instructions for setup and calibration.
Most devices come with a standard cuff, but larger or smaller sizes are sold separately. Ask your doctor or check the cuff size range in the manual. A cuff that’s too large can read low, while one that’s too small can read high.
Measurements are only as good as the technique. Sit quietly for at least five minutes before measuring without talking, scrolling a phone, or watching something stressful. Rest your arm on a table or desk with the middle of the cuff at heart level. Stay still and quiet while the device inflates. A rolled-up sleeve should not act as a tourniquet. Depending on your device, it may take a few measurements, or you may need to take measurements for a few days, recording the results, before getting a good reading.
Unless your doctor advises otherwise, take measurements first thing in the morning, about an hour after getting up, after using the bathroom, but before eating, drinking coffee, exercising, or taking blood pressure medication.
When to measure
If your blood pressure is well controlled and stable, many people check a few times a week or do a one-week round about monthly. Measuring once a day or a few times a day can put unnecessary stress on you and is usually unnecessary unless you have been advised to do so by your doctor or you have been diagnosed with high blood pressure.
When is it high?
Home readings averaging 130/80 or higher are generally considered elevated enough to discuss with a doctor. A single doctor’s office reading is only a snapshot, but a week of readings gives a reliable baseline more informative than any single number.
When to discuss with your doctor
For a very high reading without symptoms, rest five minutes and measure again; if it’s still that high, contact your doctor promptly. If you have persistent symptoms, such as headache, nausea, or palpitations, contact your doctor promptly.

In Years 7-8 the focus of the Te Reo Māori curriculum is on everyday language and tikanga (customs). Students will learn simple greetings, introductions and conversational phrases. They will also learn waiata (songs) and karakia (prayers or blessings) used in school and community settings.
They will learn the Kāi Tahu dialect spoken in Te Waipounamu (the South Island) where “k” is often used instead of “ng”. Students will therefore learn to say Kāi Tahu instead of Ngāi Tahu.
Students also have the opportunity to learn some basic phrases in other Te Reo languages such as Te Reo Reo.
The Year 9 German curriculum focuses on the basics of the language. Students learn how to introduce themselves and their families, talk about food, festivals and everyday situations. They are also taught how to tell the time and make arrangements. In Year 10 the aim is to prepare students for NCEA Level 1 and to build practical skills for use in the community. Topics covered include formal language for speeches and ceremonies, the tikanga (customs) of the marae, including pōwhiri (welcome ceremonies), the roles on the marae and appropriate behaviour. In Year 10 Te Reo Māori students learn to use the language to communicate and negotiate more effectively in their school and community contexts.
Languages are taught by specialist teachers who are fully qualified in their field and keep up to date with latest developments in language teaching. Many languages have a solid connection to our local community, allowing students to develop strong connections with their own local identities while also having a global outlook.
